protagonist.fact: Ellen is forty-nine at the story's start and turns fifty during the wedding weekend.
protagonist.evidence: "Ellen was forty-nine years old"; "the wedding was set for the last Saturday of the month, which happened to be two days before Ellen turned fifty."

protagonist.fact: She attends early church services and is embedded in a church social world.
protagonist.evidence: "She went to the early service."; "When the ladies at church talked about their husbands, Ellen would fold her hands..."

protagonist.fact: She lives alone in a small, tidy house and keeps a disciplined, routinized domestic life.
protagonist.evidence: "She kept her little house clean and still."; "Her house was dark when she got there. She let herself in..."

protagonist.fact: She has saved a 'good dress' for decades and kept an unopened letter in a shoebox on a top closet shelf for almost twenty years.
protagonist.evidence: "On the top shelf sat a shoebox she had not opened in almost twenty years."; "She kept the good dress in the closet with the tags almost worn off..."

protagonist.fact: She turned away a suitor named Thomas decades earlier and kept a letter from him unopened; the letter explains he waited three years and left because she would not open the door.
protagonist.evidence: "His name was Thomas... He had wanted to marry her. And Ellen had told him no."; "Three years I waited, hoping you would stop being afraid... I am leaving because I love you, and I cannot wait at a door you will not open."

protagonist.fact: After a pivotal conversation with an old woman, Ellen repents, changes her life, and begins living actively (painting a room, wearing the dress, reconnecting with friends).
protagonist.evidence: "You have been sitting in a locked room for thirty years... The door is open. It has always been open."; "That week she painted the spare room a warm yellow... She hung the good dress out where she could wear it... She called an old friend..."

protagonist.fact: Later she teaches a small class at church for younger women and offers counsel born of her experience.
protagonist.evidence: "She taught a little class at church for younger women, and she told them, gently, do not save your life for a day that has a name."

protagonist.fact: She meets and later forms a slow, companionate relationship with a widower named Walt; love arrives quietly and without rush.
protagonist.evidence: "He was a widower named Walt, who fixed the sound system at church and had a laugh that filled a room... There was no rush to a ring, because Ellen was already full."

relationships.fact: Niece Katie is getting married; Ellen attended her wedding.
relationships.evidence: "Her niece Katie was getting married... Katie came down the aisle..."

relationships.fact: Sister-in-law Sharon is critical under the guise of kindness and pressures Ellen about being single.
relationships.evidence: "'You will come, of course,' Sharon said... 'You are still such a lovely woman, Ellen. It is such a shame.'"; "Sharon... held her wine... 'No date tonight? ... I keep hoping.'"

relationships.fact: Her brother asked her to bring leftover flowers home for their mother and attends family dinners.
relationships.evidence: "her brother had asked her to bring the leftover flowers home for their mother."; "At the family dinner the next Sunday, her sister-in-law Sharon could not stop talking about the wedding."

relationships.fact: An elderly woman at the brunch catalyzes her awakening by telling her she locked the door herself.
relationships.evidence: "You have been waiting a long time," the old woman said... 'You have been sitting in a locked room for thirty years... The door is open. It has always been open.'"

relationships.fact: Thomas was a past suitor who loved her and left after waiting; his letter is intimate and honest.
relationships.evidence: "Before he left, he had handed her an envelope... 'Ellen. I am not leaving because I stopped loving you... I waited longer than you know. Three years I waited... Be well. Live. Please, finally, live. Tom.'"

relationships.fact: Walt is a gentle widower from church who becomes her companion.
relationships.evidence: "He was a widower named Walt, who fixed the sound system at church and had a laugh that filled a room... She was not a woman waiting to be chosen anymore. She was a woman who had finally, fully, arrived... and simply had room now for one more good thing."

social_world.fact: Ellen's social life is centered on church activities: services, ladies at church, wedding events, and church brunches.
social_world.evidence: "She went to the early service."; "When the ladies at church talked..."; "the church had a thank-you brunch for the wedding guests"

social_world.fact: Family gatherings (Sunday dinners, sibling relationships) are a regular social domain and a source of pressure.
social_world.evidence: "At the family dinner the next Sunday... Sharon could not stop talking about the wedding."

social_world.fact: Her world contains small-town-style rituals: weddings by the water, receptions, and neighborhood familiarity.
social_world.evidence: "The flowers, the dress, the venue by the water."; "She sat in the third row, on the aisle, in the seat where they put the ones who came alone."

whole_script_vibe.social_class_and_lifestyle: Modest middle-class, financially independent with simple comforts; church-centered, small-town or close-knit suburban life.
whole_script_vibe.professional_energy: Steady, routine-oriented, responsible; not career-ambitious but reliable and conscientious.
whole_script_vibe.primary_visual_vibe: Warm, domestic, sunlit interiors; quiet composure with moments of emotional release; textures like worn fabric, well-kept wood, and soft light on water.
whole_script_vibe.wardrobe_vibe: Conservative, classic, comfortable: soft knits, practical skirts or simple dresses, neutral palettes with one sentimental 'good dress' kept for years.
credible_locations: community college or municipal administrative office
coastal wedding venue or lakefront park
local café or church brunch room

abstract_casting_signals.economic_independence: modestly financially independent; owns a small home and manages on steady income/savings
abstract_casting_signals.interpersonal_style: quietly warm, attentive, sometimes self-effacing but capable of firm honesty
abstract_casting_signals.cultural_tone: Christian, small-town/suburban American with traditional social rituals

cinematic_inference.protagonist_occupation: Municipal Landscape Planner / Residential Streetscape Designer
cinematic_inference.body_design: 5'6" (168 cm), medium build with broad shoulders and a steady, upright carriage; hands with visible calluses and a faint old scrape along the knuckle of the right index finger.
cinematic_inference.ethnicity_design: White American of Northern European descent, with a slightly weathered, fair complexion and light freckling from years outdoors.
cinematic_inference.hair_design: Salt-and-pepper hair cut into a short, wavy bob that tucks behind the ears; usually pinned back with a simple tortoiseshell barrette when in the field.
cinematic_inference.wardrobe_design: Smart-casual conservative: durable waxed-cotton field jacket in olive, neutral wool cardigan, chambray button-up shirts, tailored khaki chinos, low-profile leather ankle boots for site work, and a neat pair of reading glasses on a cord. For public meetings she adds a lightweight blazer and a modest silver pendant; accessories are minimal and practical (weatherproof notebook, folding tape measure, leather satchel).
cinematic_inference.casting_rationale: The Municipal Landscape Planner role matches the subject’s patient, methodical temperament and steady, collaborative work style while providing a tactile, visually rich world for film—site visits, community meetings, and hands-on problem solving. The wardrobe and body details convey someone comfortable both in the field and at a town table: practical, quietly professional, and physically believable without dramatic extremes.

stable_identity: Late 40s–early 60s female municipal landscape planner who owns a modest suburban bungalow
Methodical, quietly warm, and steadfast—approaches problems with patience and clear priorities
Religiously culturally Christian in small-town rituals but not professionally tied to religious institutions
director_profile.social_dynamics: Works within a small municipal office and regularly interfaces with homeowners, public works engineers, volunteer garden groups, and a few reliable contractors; she is respected for steady judgement, often defuses heated community meetings with calm pragmatism, and has one close colleague (a younger civil engineer) who challenges her assumptions gently.
director_profile.professional_vibe: Practical design sensibility that balances aesthetics and maintenance realities; prefers incremental, negotiated improvements over sweeping gestures and keeps thorough, well-organized records and sketches.
director_profile.visual_vibe: Earth-toned, tactile palettes—muddy boots, clipped plant notes, rolled-up plans, printed CAD overlays, seed catalogs, and seasonal shifts from spring planting color to muted winter textures; light often finds her on porches or beside newly planted curbs.
credible_worlds: Town hall meetings in a modest municipal building with folding chairs and a projector
Residential streetscapes—narrow sidewalks, mature maples, front porches where she sketches plans and talks with homeowners
Fieldwork scenes at dawn or after rain—measuring curbs, directing a planting crew, inspecting stormwater trenches
director_profile.parallel_story_rule: Any subplot should not make her profession the plot’s moral center; instead, use her job as a grounded arena where personal values are shown through decisions, small acts of care, and steady negotiation rather than didactic speeches or institutional authority.

occupation_selection.job_title: Municipal Landscape Planner / Residential Streetscape Designer
occupation_selection.rationale:
This role fits the profile’s steady, methodical temperament and quietly collaborative interpersonal style while offering a visually rich, active world for film. It supports a modest, reliable income and independent lifestyle without tying the character to family or religious institutions. The planner’s work is thoughtful and patient—listening to neighbors, negotiating with public-works crews, and balancing design ideals with practical constraints—which suits a reserved, steadfast protagonist who can be warm but firm.

Cinematically, the job provides varied locations and movement: site visits on tree-lined suburban streets, sketching plans on front porches, walking construction sites in sensible shoes, meeting in town-hall rooms and around kitchen tables, and seasonal contrasts (planting in spring, brown winter yards, stormwater features after rain). It supports active scenes (measuring, directing crews, calming anxious homeowners, presenting to a small board), a range of relationships (homeowners, municipal engineers, contractors, volunteer groups), and changing environments that reveal character (a quiet survey at dawn, a tense public hearing, hands dirty in the soil). The visual palette—maps, plant catalogs, CAD printouts, muddy boots, flowering beds—gives filmmakers texture and motion while staying true to the character’s steady, methodical work style.
